classification.difficultyReason: Apply the one-output-per-input condition to four familiar graph shapes, including two relations with repeated x-coordinates.

content.prompt: Determine which of the following relations are functions.

spec.description: Left semicircle with included endpoints on the y-axis; equal coordinate units preserve its semicircular shape.
spec.mathematics: x²+y²=4 with x≤0; endpoints (0,2) and (0,−2) included.
spec.answerVisibility: The source relation is permanently visible; classification appears only in answers.

answer.worked: The points $(0,2)$ and $(0,-2)$ have the same $x$-coordinate but different $y$-coordinates. One input therefore has two outputs, so the relation is not a function.

spec.description: Unspecified cubic-shaped relation reconstructed with smooth curves, preserving its intercepts, turning directions and continuation arrows without asserting an unprovided equation.
spec.mathematics: A continuous single-valued curve crossing the x-axis at −2, 0 and 2; local minimum between −2 and 0 and local maximum between 0 and 2.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied relation is visible in the question.

answer.worked: Each $x$-coordinate has exactly one corresponding $y$-coordinate. No input has two outputs, so the relation is a function.

spec.description: Reciprocal branches in quadrants II and IV, with axes as asymptotes and dashed guides to the two supplied coordinate pairs.
spec.mathematics: Reciprocal curve through (−2,2) and (2,−2), reconstructed as y=−4/x; x=0 is excluded.
spec.answerVisibility: The equation used to construct the curve is not printed.

answer.worked: For each $x$-coordinate on the relation, there is exactly one $y$-coordinate. There is no point with $x=0$, but no input in the domain has two outputs. The relation is a function.

spec.description: Vertical line through x=2, with continuation arrows at both ends.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied line and axis labels are visible in the question.

answer.worked: The input $x=2$ corresponds to many different $y$-coordinates. One input has more than one output, so the relation is not a function.
